episode_title: 373 - Giving Less F_cks About My Clients’ Results Made Me Richer & A Better Coach

real_qa.q: How did shifting responsibility to clients impact Jill Parekh's coaching business revenue and capacity?
real_qa.r: The more responsibility Jill gave back to her clients, the more capacity she had to make more money and sign more people and impact more clients. The better her coaching relationships became because they were no longer contingent on her over-delivering or acting a certain way to ensure client happiness. She realized that her previous self-sacrifice and over-extension were not actually serving anybody and were communicating that her coaching wasn't enough.
real_qa.requete: Jill Parekh giving responsibility to clients revenue

real_qa.q: Why does obsessing over client results create codependency in coaching relationships?
real_qa.r: When coaches obsess over client results and over-deliver emotionally, they create codependent relationships and energetically expect clients to feel a certain way about it. This behavior communicates that the coach doesn't trust clients and needs to constantly intervene. Jill spent 90% of her day making sure her clients were happy and never upset with her, which blocked her from signing more clients and limited her capacity to impact more people.

real_qa.q: How should coaches separate their self-worth from client outcomes according to Jill Parekh?
real_qa.r: Coaches must recognize that their confidence and identity become hostage to their clients' results. The most successful business owners only believe their self-concept is contingent on themselves—not on clients or external validation. Jill learned that thinking you can control client outcomes is 'a losing fucking game' because you cannot control someone else's actions, feelings, and results; you are not God.

real_qa.q: What percentage of clients typically slip through the cracks and don't achieve results in coaching?
real_qa.r: Jill states that while most clients can get phenomenal results, you will have clients that don't get results, and this represents a small percentage. She emphasizes that life happens, hardships occur, or clients realize they don't actually want to do the thing they're doing. She also references a former coach who claimed a 100% success rate until Jill became her client and saw 'massive amounts of people who didn't get fucking results in working with her.'
real_qa.requete: coaching success rate small percentage clients

real_qa.q: How does client celebration frequency affect a coach's ability to sell their offer authentically?
real_qa.r: Jill noticed a stark difference in how she sold based on whether clients were sharing wins that week. When she received screenshots of client results, she would sell with maximum power and conviction. But when the wins channel was empty for a couple weeks, she couldn't talk about the offer with the same belief, thinking clients weren't doing well. This fear of selling without perfect client results undermined her power and effectiveness in marketing.
real_qa.requete: client wins impact coach selling power conviction

guest.bio_context: Jill Parekh is a 34-year-old business owner with a stuttering disability who has built a multiple six-figure business through online coaching and content creation. She specializes in helping clients overcome imposter syndrome and self-doubt while building their personal brands and revenue. Her coaching practice includes group masterminds that meet on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and she hosts the Did I Stutter?! podcast.
